intro: The Dhammapada is small enough to carry in a pocket and old enough to have been memorized for more than two thousand years. Its 423 verses are short. Many fit on one line. Yet Buddhist teachers have spent whole lifetimes explaining them.

In this unit you will read the Dhammapada closely in F. Max Muller's 1881 translation, which is in the public domain. You will read its famous opening pairs, its chapter on the mind, and its chapters on the fool, the wise, the thousands, the self, anger and the Brahmana. You will compare Muller's words with modern translations and meet the commentary stories behind the verses.

By the end, you will be able to close read a verse: its words, its neighbors, its Pali key term and its readers. You will also be able to explain how Buddhist teachers fit a line like 'self is the lord of self' with the teaching of not-self, without deciding the question for anyone.
bigQuestion: How do short verses carry a whole way of life, and how do readers decide what they mean?

timeline.t: The Buddha's death, on many scholars' dates; sayings begin to be passed on by memory
Ashoka's reign; Buddhist teaching spreads, and monks reach Sri Lanka
The Pali Canon, including the Dhammapada, written down in Sri Lanka, as chronicles report
The Gandhari Dharmapada, a related collection, is copied on birch bark
The Dhammapada commentary, credited to Buddhaghosa, gathers stories for each verse
Viggo Fausboll publishes the Pali text with a Latin translation
F. Max Muller's English translation appears in Sacred Books of the East 10
E.W. Burlingame translates the commentary stories as Buddhist Legends
J.R. Jayewardene quotes verse 5 at the San Francisco peace conference
Acharya Buddharakkhita's modern translation is published

words.d: a Pali collection of 423 verses in 26 chapters
the paired verses of the Dhammapada's first chapter
mind; the key word of verse 1
mind or heart; the subject of chapter 3
by non-hatred; Muller renders it 'by love' in verse 5
a later text that explains an earlier one, such as the Dhammapada stories
not-self: no permanent, unchanging self is found in body or mind
ordinary speech, like 'I,' that teachers say is useful but not ultimate
upekkha: a mind not tipped by praise or blame
a brahmin; in chapter 26, a person worthy by conduct, not birth

test.q: How many verses does the Dhammapada contain?
test.why: The Dhammapada has 423 verses in 26 chapters.

test.q: Who translated the Dhammapada in SBE 10 (1881)?
test.why: Muller's translation appeared in Sacred Books of the East 10.

test.q: In verse 1, what follows a person who acts with an evil thought?
choices: Pain, as a wheel follows the ox
test.why: Verse 1 uses the image of the wheel and the ox.
Happiness follows a pure thought like a shadow.

test.q: In verse 3, what keeps hatred alive?
choices: Harbouring thoughts of wrongs done to oneself
test.why: Hatred never ceases in those who harbour such thoughts.

test.q: What does Muller's 'love' in verse 5 translate?
What does verse 33 compare training the mind to?
test.why: Verse 33: as a fletcher makes straight his arrow.

test.q: What does the commentary story of Cakkhupala stress?
test.why: The blind monk did no wrong because he had no intention to kill.

test.q: Who does verse 63 call 'a fool indeed'?
choices: A fool who thinks himself wise
test.why: Verse 63 names the fool who thinks himself wise.

test.q: Which verse says 'self is the lord of self'?
test.why: Verse 160 in chapter 12, on the self.

test.q: Which idea do many teachers use to fit verse 160 with not-self?
test.why: They read 'self' in verse 160 as ordinary speech.

test.q: In verse 222, who is the real driver?
choices: One who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot
test.why: Verse 222 praises the one who checks anger.

test.q: How does chapter 26 define a brahmana?
test.why: The Brahmana chapter redefines the title by conduct.

test.q: What does verse 103 call the greatest conquest?
test.why: One who conquers himself is the greatest conqueror.

test.q: What is the best first step before comparing the Dhammapada with another scripture?
choices: Read it in its own terms and setting
test.why: Reading each text in its own terms keeps comparison fair.

write.prompt: What does the Dhammapada say about how a person should respond to harm? Cite two or three verses (for example 3, 5, 222 and 223, Muller's SBE 10, 1881), explain what each says, and describe how two readers, such as a commentary and a modern translator, read them.
tips: Give the verse number and the translator each time you quote.
Read each verse's neighbors before you explain it.
Attribute every reading: 'Muller renders…', 'Theravada teachers read…'.
Note any key Pali word, such as averena, and how translators differ.
